extracted.intended_audience: student journalists (WJEA News Writing Write-Off contestants and school news staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing breaking-news stories for school news outlets and the WJEA News Writing Write-Off, focusing on structure, timeliness, sourcing, style, and presentation. Advises when to use inverted-pyramid breaking-news format versus feature writing for school papers and how to post/update quickly online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the inverted pyramid structure with a summary lede
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing style for breaking news typically follows the inverted pyramid structure with a summary lede that includes the who, what, where and when.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overview reference to Poynter article provided. Examples from Penn State Collegian and CNN illustrate the approach. The inverted pyramid places the basics first, with more specific details later in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the 4 W's in the summary lede
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary lede should include who, what, where and when.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lede should convey the essential facts (4 W's) but not overload with too many specifics that can overwhelm readers; use the body to expand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise in the lede—avoid excessive specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: The lede should convey the basics first and avoid too many specific details which can overwhelm readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: CNN's lede included the 4 W's but did not include too many specifics. Save details for subsequent paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post breaking items ASAP on school news websites
rubrics_metrics.description: If something 'breaking' occurs (snow day, sports or activity victories, lockdown, new principal announced, schedules changed, etc.), student journalists should post it ASAP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inverted pyramid is the standard way to reach busy readers online. Timeliness and prompt posting are important for breaking news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce a concise lede suitable for social posting
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary lede can even be abbreviated and sent as a 140-character tweet before or when the full story is posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the tweet-sized lede for immediate notification while the fuller inverted-pyramid story provides more context on the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate approach: feature writing vs. breaking-news style
rubrics_metrics.description: School newspapers are unlikely to contain actual breaking news, so a feature-writing approach tends to work best for print papers, while school news websites should contain breaking news written in inverted-pyramid style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select feature storytelling for most school-paper pieces; reserve inverted-pyramid, summary-lede format for true breaking items on news websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep paragraphs very short in the story body
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short paragraphs help readability for busy readers and for online consumption; break text into bite-sized chunks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use expressive quotes and punctuate/attribute them properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use expressive quotes, if available, and properly punctuate and attribute them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose vivid, relevant quotations that add voice or facts; ensure correct punctuation and clear attribution to the speaker/source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute information to sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell readers where you are getting your information (attribute info to sources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear sourcing builds credibility; explicitly attribute statements, facts, and official information to named sources or agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow AP Style (use WJEA AP Style cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow AP Style. Use the WJEA AP Style 'cheat sheet' as a starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhering to AP Style ensures consistency and professionalism in news writing; consult the cheat sheet for common rules used by WJEA.
